title: The Fed Chair Never Loses a Vote: Warsh Talks Against Guidance, but His Body Is Already Paving the Way for Hikes
dek: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, arguing that he talks against forward guidance while actually paving the way for hikes, and predicts the Fed will raise rates 75-100 basis points over the next six months.
why: Posen is one of the few central bank watchers willing to say 'fiscal dominance' out loud. This episode offers hard judgments on Fed governance risk, Powell's record, and AI's impact on jobs, with high information density.
who: Macro traders watching the Fed's path, economists studying AI's impact on employment, and policy researchers concerned about central bank independence.
skip: The final two minutes of subscription and Discord promotion can be skipped.

points.h: Warsh didn't say he'd hike, but the whole speech paved the way
points.body: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, but says it could be treated as a B+ given the chaos of the preceding two months. The fourth section systematically lists reasons inflation could persist or even rise, yet never says 'therefore we must tighten.' Posen sees this as deliberate groundwork: if hikes don't follow, the market will suspect a capitulation to Trump. Posen himself has argued for hikes for months because inflation is real. Warsh also made clear a 2% core PCE target and refused to use wage inflation as a forecasting indicator—both mainstream moves.

points.h: Without defining the 'right speed,' returning to target is empty talk
points.body: Posen's biggest worry is that Warsh ended the speech saying inflation needs to fall in the 'right direction' at the 'right speed,' yet never defines what the right speed is. Without a speed constraint, 'returning to target' is empty talk. From his confirmation hearing to two press conferences to the ECB Sintra speech, Warsh has consistently reserved the right to decide at the last minute, refusing to pre-commit to his own watch indicators. This is close to Greenspan's 1999 style, but Greenspan held it together through personal ability and control of the committee; one mistake and the whole credibility collapses.

points.h: The Fed chair never loses a vote
points.body: Posen explains the Fed committee culture: unlike the ECB's pursuit of consensus, the Fed has historically given the chair more power. More crucially, there's an unwritten rule—only a few dissent at each meeting, and the chair never loses a vote. When Volcker found he might lose a vote, he simply announced it would be his last meeting. This culture makes the committee weak at correcting the chair, so Warsh's 'preserve discretion' style carries more risk than he imagines.

points.h: Criticizing the central bank isn't dangerous; making it help sell Treasuries is
points.body: Posen distinguishes two types of political pressure: ordinary criticism of the central bank is part of the game and can even help it 'take the heat' when necessary. The real danger is when a president or treasury secretary asks the central bank to help sell government bonds; the central bank must then answer: 'I am here to help you and your successor sell bonds,' and must never manipulate or cheat. Trump's threats to the Fed are far more serious than rhetoric—trying to strip regional Fed presidents of voting rights, disrupt staggered terms, change the mandate, and touch the budget directly undermine functional independence.

points.h: The most radical reform might be making the central bank talk less
points.body: Posen thinks the communications committee led by Mervyn King is most likely to produce radical proposals. King himself is a founder of inflation targeting and fan charts, but after retirement he publicly doubted the central bank's forecasting ability and information supply: too much noise makes markets rely on official guidance, creating moral hazard and bubbles. Peter Fisher agrees, arguing that central bank 'certainty' reduces market risk sensitivity. The two could push for less information dissemination, not more. Warsh's 'hall of mirrors' metaphor in the speech already admits the market may not be right.

points.h: Economists who join AI companies lose their independent voice
points.body: Posen argues that economists flocking to AI companies is not unprecedented—it happened during the internet era—but this time it's more troubling. Companies like Anthropic hire economists partly to design AI transition policies, and these scholars genuinely believe they're doing good. The problem is that once inside, they enter the corporate hierarchy, lose their independent voice and freedom to choose topics, and their views get reasonably discounted by outsiders. Posen's hope is that scholars stay in research institutes, earn low six-figure salaries, and still have public influence.

points.h: AI replacement hasn't happened yet; programmer employment is still growing
points.body: Posen says labor market data doesn't yet show AI replacement; even employment growth for programmers and truck drivers continues. Brynjolfsson's J-curve theory holds that firms need time to reorganize, and humans and AI will first have a cooperative period. Garicano's messy jobs theory points out that the jobs most easily automated actually contain a lot of tacit knowledge and human relationships—for example, a truck driver doesn't just drive. Large-scale replacement may take about five years, and will first show up in reduced hiring of young people.

points.h: In six months rates will be 75-100 basis points higher than now
points.body: Posen reiterates his earlier forecast of 4% year-end PCE inflation, which is materializing; CPI already exceeded 4% early this year. The bigger problem is inflation inertia: although energy prices may bring the next month or two's figures down slightly, core services inflation is stubborn, with 3/6/12-month moving averages all rising. He expects the Fed to hike in September or December; if it hikes in September, it will hike again in December, and in six months the federal funds rate will be 75-100 basis points higher than now, only then will inflation truly start to fall, and during that period it will be in the 3.5%-4.5% range.
